en: Pounding steamed glutinous rice into sticky tikoy is a physical change because the grains change shape without forming new chemical substances.
Leaving coconut sap out in the sun causes it to ferment into tuba vinegar through a chemical change that produces new substances.
A bowl of halo-halo containing shaved ice, sweet beans, and purple yam is a heterogeneous mixture because you can easily see its different parts.
Squeezing calamansi juice and dissolving sugar in water creates a homogeneous solution where the citrus and sweet particles spread evenly throughout the liquid.
Capiz shells are used as translucent window panels in old Filipino houses because they allow light to pass through while scattering it softly.
Abaca plant fibers possess high tensile strength, making them an excellent natural material for manufacturing strong Manila ropes used in shipping.
Water vapor in the cool Baguio morning air undergoes condensation to form liquid dew drops on the needles of Benguet pine trees.
Solid mothballs placed inside a traditional Filipino kamagong wood cabinet undergo sublimation to directly turn into a gas that protects clothes from weevils.
Dissolving solid rock salt in a hot pot of sinigang broth is a physical change because the salt particles just spread out without forming new substances.
The iron roof of a nipa hut in coastal Batangas undergoes a chemical change called oxidation when it reacts with salty sea air to form rust.
Hollow bamboo poles float on the Pasig River because the trapped air inside makes the overall density of the bamboo lower than the water.
Liquid mango juice placed inside a freezer undergoes freezing to become solid mango popsicles commonly sold in Philippine neighborhoods.
